extracted.intended_audience: teachers, curriculum designers, education students, and educational theorists
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and evaluative criteria for selecting subject matter and organizing method in school instruction, aimed at aligning classroom activity with learners' experience, social purpose, and scientific method. Emphasizes teacher role, stages of learner knowledge, and inclusion of active occupations (play and work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Traits of good method
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressed in terms of the attitude of the individual the traits of good method are straightforwardness, flexible intellectual interest or open-minded will to learn, integrity of purpose, and acceptance of responsibility for the consequences of one's activity including thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method is derived from observation of the course of experiences where there is no conscious distinction of personal attitude and manner from material dealt with. Methods are individualized, but these traits may be discriminated because of prior experiences and general similarities in materials. Avoid conceiving method as separate, formal, mechanical, or constrained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid division between avowed/public and private mental life
rubrics_metrics.description: A split between avowed, public, socially responsible undertakings and private, ill-regulated, and suppressed indulgences of thought hampers integrity and completeness of mental action, constrains reflective dealings with instructional material, and demoralizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causes include 'stern discipline,' extrinsic rewards, schooling treated merely as preparatory, and exaggerated drill. Consequences: attention wanders to furtive topics, impulses enter action unacknowledged, and habits form that make vital mental qualities less available for public ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid external coercive pressure and extrinsic rewards
rubrics_metrics.description: External coercive pressure ('stern discipline') and motivation through rewards extraneous to the thing to be done tend to split mind and undermine responsible, integrated thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These practices produce superficial compliance and force pupils to find other illicit outlets for desires and affections; they weaken the discipline that comes from regulating response by deliberate inquiry and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Responsibility as an element in intellectual attitude is the disposition to consider in advance the probable consequences of any projected step and deliberately to accept them: to take them into account and acknowledge them in action, not yielding a mere verbal assent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fewer facts worked through into situations where conviction means real identification of self with required conduct is preferable to many superficially accepted truths. Intellectual responsibility requires severe standards and practice in following up and acting upon the meaning of what is acquired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual thoroughness (seeing a thing through)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual thoroughness is seeing a thing through; it depends upon a unity of purpose to which details are subordinated, not upon a multitude of disconnected details or purely mechanical drill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is manifested in the firmness with which the full meaning of the purpose is developed. Distinguish this from mechanical/exhausting drill which produces automatic skill without engaged thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method should derive from natural course of experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Method is a statement of the way the subject matter of an experience develops most effectively and fruitfully; it is derived from observation of experiences where personal attitude and material are not consciously distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat method as integrated with the learner's active experience; avoid treating method as an external formula. While individualized, method shares features observable from prior experiences and material similarities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher's knowledge must mediate adult subject-matter and pupil experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The educator's knowledge of subject matter beyond the pupil's is to supply definite standards and to reveal possibilities of the crude activities of the immature; teacher should perceive inchoate impulses and provide stimuli to direct them into educative action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The teacher's task is to focus on the interplay of subject matter with pupils' present needs and capacities; simple scholarship is insufficient and the adult organization of material can obstruct effective teaching unless adapted to the learner's experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject matter must supply an environment to form desirable dispositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter consists of facts and ideas developed in the course of a situation having a purpose; the educator furnishes environments that stimulate responses and direct learners so that desirable intellectual and emotional dispositions form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subject matter in formal instruction should connect with social life (stories, traditions, songs) and be selected, formulated, and organized so it can be transmitted in ways that relate to pupils' activities and social uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stages in development of subject matter for the learner
rubrics_metrics.description: Three typical stages: (I) knowledge as intelligent ability or 'know-how' (power to do); (II) information communicated (facts and reports that supplement acquaintance); (III) science or rationalized, logically organized knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curriculum design should recognize these stages—start from doing, then build informative communications tied to pupil concerns, and finally work toward scientific organization and method as pupils mature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for informational material to be educative
rubrics_metrics.description: Informational material is educative if (1) it grows naturally out of some question with which the student is concerned, and (2) it fits into his more direct acquaintance so as to increase its efficacy and deepen its meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If informational material fails these two requirements it becomes mere words—verbal stimuli lacking meaning—and tends to produce memorization, mechanical reactions, and superficial acquaintance rather than genuine learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit quantity; prioritize applicability and organization over bulk of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive bulk of communicated subject matter (facts, histories, treatises) can swamp pupils and convert knowledge into mere verbal memory; quantity is not of prime importance unless the student has a need for it and can apply it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer fewer things intellectually worked out so conviction is real; avoid cramming and rote memorization; emphasize organization of material into the learner's experience rather than encyclopedic coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach science as method and guard against its aloofness
rubrics_metrics.description: Science is rationalized knowledge whose organization follows from adequate methods of tested discovery; initiation into scientific spirit is essential but scientific results taken alone may be remote and abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should present science as a method of inquiry (logical warranty, mutual implication of conceptions) and connect scientific organization with students' experience to avoid abstract, unmotivated presentations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select curriculum by social worth; place essentials first
rubrics_metrics.description: With many possible materials to select from, education should use a criterion of social worth: adapt studies to the needs of existing community life, select to improve common life, and place socially fundamental essentials before specialized refinements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor broadly human criteria (materials connecting with common interests of men as men) over narrowly utilitarian training for unchosen labor or cultivation for an elite. Present situations relevant to living together to develop social insight and interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include play and work (active occupations) in the curriculum
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms of activity in play and work similar to those children engage in outside school engage the whole pupil: they bring natural impulses into play, make school a joy, reduce managerial burden, and make learning easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Play and constructive occupations should not be mere diversions; they provide motives for attention, reduce gap between school and life, promote cooperative associations in a social setting, and afford educative engagement with materials and processes.
